name: Repulsons and Massless Black Holes
description: The static, supersymmetric, charged solutions of the heterotic string reduced to four dimensions whose naked singularity turns back every massive particle, found by Klaus Behrndt, by Renata Kallosh and Andrei Linde, and by Mirjam Cvetič and Donam Youm in 1995. Gravity attracts far away and repels inside a radius set by the mass and the charge, and with the mass zero it repels at every radius and space is still curved.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and $M$ and $q$ are lengths, Kallosh and Linde's mass and charge in units with $G = 1$ and the dilaton zero at infinity [kallosh1995white]. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Repulsons are static, supersymmetric solutions of the heterotic string whose naked singularity reflects every massive particle that falls toward it [kallosh1995white]. Some of them have zero mass measured from far away, and the space around them is still curved [behrndt1995, kallosh1995white]. Andrew Strominger had argued in April 1995 that black holes of type II string theory become massless at a conifold point of a Calabi-Yau space, where the surfaces their branes wrap shrink to zero area [strominger1995massless]. Klaus Behrndt, at the Humboldt University in Berlin, gave the first explicit solution of this kind in June 1995, from a model of the heterotic string reduced to four dimensions [behrndt1995, kallosh1995white]. The holes lose their mass at the point where the model is its own T-dual, and Behrndt identified them with string states of left moving oscillator number $N_L = 0$ [behrndt1995].¶Renata Kallosh, at Stanford, found a curvature singularity in the massless solution, at a radius where its dilaton diverges [kallosh1995duality]. There the volume of the six rolled up dimensions shrinks to zero, and the solution in ten dimensions is smooth [behrndt1995, kallosh1995white]. Kallosh and Andrei Linde gave the electrically charged solutions in July 1995, $$ds^2 = -\Delta^{-1/2}dt^2 + \Delta^{1/2}(dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2), \qquad \Delta = 1 + \frac{4M}{r} - \frac{4q^2}{r^2},$$ in units with $G = c = 1$ and the dilaton zero at infinity, for mass $M \ge 0$ and charge $q$ [kallosh1995white]. Its singularity lies at $r_0 = 2(\sqrt{M^2 + q^2} - M)$, and inside $r_c = 2q^2/M$ gravity repels, with a force that grows without bound toward $r_0$ [kallosh1995white]. A massive particle falling in turns back before it reaches $r_0$, and with $M = 0$ the force repels at every radius [kallosh1995white]. Kallosh and Linde called the solutions "supersymmetric white holes, or repulsons", and took "repulsons" from a suggestion of their referee [kallosh1995white].¶Mirjam Cvetič and Donam Youm, at the University of Pennsylvania, found the same repulsion in July 1995 among their static solutions with two electric and two magnetic charges [cvetic1995singular]. When the two charges of one kind have opposite signs the solutions are singular, and when the charges of each such pair are equal in size the mass vanishes [cvetic1995singular]. The electric ones that become massless at the self dual radius of a circle are elementary string states, and they enlarge a gauge symmetry $U(1) \times U(1)$ to $U(1) \times SU(2)$ [cvetic1995singular]. Massless test particles with no angular momentum reach the singularity in a finite time [cvetic1995singular]. Tomás Ortín, at CERN, described the massless hole in 1996 as an extreme black hole of dilaton coupling $a = \sqrt{3}$ bound to a singular object of equal and opposite mass [ortin1996]. At one point the pair gives the massless metric, a dihole in Ortín's word, and two diholes at one point give a quadruhole [ortin1996].¶Supersymmetry forbids isolated objects of negative mass, Ortín wrote, "but it does not forbid their existence in non-negative mass bound states, just as quarks do not exist in isolation at low energies" [ortin1996]. Kallosh and Linde showed in 1996 that the Coulomb and scalar forces between such states cancel, so pairs of oppositely charged massless states can be added with no change in energy [kallosh1996balance]. Roberto Emparan, at Santa Barbara, found a solution in 1996 in which two massless holes of opposite charge move with uniform acceleration and no external force acts on them [emparan1996]. Continued to Euclidean time, the solution is an instanton for the production of such pairs in flat space, and its negative action enhances that production [emparan1996]. If the holes were allowed, the vacuum of flat space would be "highly unstable against their production in pairs" [emparan1996].¶Ingo Gaida, at Cambridge, probed the singularity with a quantum scalar field in 1998 and found it transparent to the field [gaida1998]. With Helia Hollmann and John Stewart, Gaida found in 1999 that the field is reflected at $r = 0$ [gaida1999]. Clifford Johnson, Amanda Peet, and Joseph Polchinski studied in 2000 a dual of the magnetic repulsons in type II string theory, D6-branes wrapped on a K3 surface that gives them a negative D2-brane charge [johnson2000]. A wrapped D6-brane sent in as a probe loses its tension at a radius $r_{\rm e}$ outside the singularity, so the branes stop there and form a shell [johnson2000]. The geometry inside the shell is cut out and replaced by flat space, in which an $SU(2)$ gauge symmetry is unbroken [johnson2000]. For that symmetry Johnson, Peet, and Polchinski called the geometry the enhançon geometry [johnson2000].¶Johnson, Robert Myers, Peet, and Simon Ross showed in 2001 that the excision is consistent in gravity alone, and that the shell joining the two geometries behaves as wrapped D6-branes whose tension vanishes at $r_{\rm e}$ [johnson2001]. Makoto Natsuume found the same shell in 2002 in the heterotic string itself, at the radius where a circle reaches its self dual size [natsuume2002]. Pablo A. Cano, Samuele Chimento, Tomás Ortín, and Alejandro Ruipérez added in 2019 the corrections of first order in the string parameter $\alpha'$ to massless holes with four charges [cano2019]. The corrected hole has a mass $\alpha'/8Q$ for charges of size $Q$, a horizon, and no singularity, and its spacetime continues into further asymptotically flat regions of positive and negative mass [cano2019]. In ten dimensions the corrected configuration is still singular, and Cano, Chimento, Ortín, and Ruipérez left open how seriously string theory should take it [cano2019].

related.text: The black holes of Cvetič and Youm with four charges, the two of each kind of one sign, which have horizons. With the two charges of one kind of opposite sign the same solutions are singular and repel massive particles [cvetic1995singular].

The magnetic black hole of coupling $a = 1$ is, in the heterotic string, a Kaluza-Klein monopole together with an H-monopole [johnson2000]. With the two magnetic charges of opposite sign the pair is singular and repels massive particles [cvetic1995singular].

With $q = 0$ the electric solution of Kallosh and Linde is the extreme electric hole of coupling $a = \sqrt{3}$, with $\Delta = 1 + 4M/r$ [kallosh1995white]. Ortín made the massless hole from one of these holes and a partner of opposite charge and negative mass, placed at one point [ortin1996].
A magnetic repulson of Cvetič and Youm is a Kaluza-Klein monopole bound to an H-monopole whose magnetic charge has the opposite sign [cvetic1995singular].
Behrndt's stationary solutions of the heterotic string are a string version of these metrics, and their static limit is the Majumdar-Papapetrou black hole [behrndt1995].
The charged black hole of Einstein-Maxwell theory. Gravity repels near its timelike singularity as near the repulson's, and near that of Schwarzschild's solution with negative mass [cano2019].
With negative mass its singularity is naked and repels [cano2019]. The repulson's singularity acts on test particles "as a body with a negative mass", in Kallosh and Linde's words [kallosh1995white].

The time reverse of a collapse, the older meaning of the name. Kallosh and Linde called the repulsons white holes because they reflect every massive particle, and used "repulsons" to avoid this meaning [kallosh1995white].

coordinates.name: Einstein Metric, Isotropic

parameters.description: Mass as a length, in units with $G = c = 1$; $M \ge 0$, and $M = 0$ is the massless repulson
Charge as a length, in units with $G = c = 1$ and the dilaton zero at infinity
Metric function, a pure number, zero at the singularity $r_0 = 2\left(\sqrt{M^2 + q^2} - M\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use the isotropic coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Kallosh and Linde's Einstein metric [kallosh1995white], with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $\lambda$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

parameters.description: Mass as a length, in units with $G = c = 1$; $M \ge 0$, and $M = 0$ is the massless repulson

coordinates.convention: We use the same coordinates on the string metric $e^{2\varphi}g_{\mu\nu}$ of Kallosh and Linde [kallosh1995white], with $g_{\mu\nu}$ the Einstein metric and $e^{-2\varphi} = \sqrt{\Delta}$ the dilaton, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $\lambda$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
